sources: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, Silverfish and Firebrats (Zygentoma) fact sheet, K. Dugas: primitive wingless insects from an ancient lineage; scales give a silvery look; two antennae and three tail filaments; hide in cracks by day, active at night; silverfish prefer cool humid places such as basements, firebrats warm places near furnaces and heating ducts; feed mainly on starch including glue, paste and paper, scraping off individual layers until paper is tissue-thin with ragged holes; 3 months to 2 years to develop; adults keep molting all their lives; lower humidity, store paper in dry airtight containers, discard unused cardboard and old newspapers; https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/publications/fact_sheets/entomology/silverfish_firebrats_zygentoma.pdf

University of Maryland, Bug of the Week (Prof. Michael J. Raupp), 'Ancient insect in a modern world: silverfish': among the most ancient of insects, 'a creature older than dinosaurs'; eats paper, book glue and natural fabrics, also cereals and preserved meat, and dead insects including other silverfish; pests in libraries and museums; https://bugoftheweek.com/blog/2021/2/12/ancient-insect-in-a-modern-world-silverfish-lepismatidae
Penn State Extension, House Centipedes: house centipedes feed on silverfish, firebrats, cockroaches and spiders; https://extension.psu.edu/house-centipedes

beats.say: Number thirteen. Silverfish. No wings, covered in silver scales, and older than dinosaurs.
It eats starch. Glue, paste, and paper.
It scrapes off one thin layer at a time, until your pages turn to tissue, full of holes.
By day, it hides in cracks. At night, it comes out. It loves cool, damp basements.
In libraries and museums, it's a real pest.
Silverfish. D tier. A nuisance for your books and papers.
